We do this across three style dimensions (formality, politeness, and intimacy) and twelve directed language pairs, measuring style alignment with the correlation-based metric $\mathcal{A}$. We find that fine-tuning does not reliably improve alignment: the three variants are statistically indistinguishable in aggregate. The open backbone does not match RASTA-GPT-4 overall, but the shortfall is concentrated in formality and largely closes for intimacy and Chinese directions, where the open model matches or surpasses GPT-4 on individual pairs. An accessible RASTA pipeline built on an open model is thus already viable for parts of the problem.
  </details>

- **[Composable Parametric Demographic Injection for Values Survey Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23867)**  `arXiv:2610.23867`  
  _Xinyuan Cao, Qingyi Pan, Bangde Du, Yujia Zhou, Hexi Wang, Weihang Su, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as simulated respondents in computational social science, yet accurately reproducing population-specific heterogeneous response distributions remains challenging. Existing methods such as demographic prompting are sensitive to prompt design and increase inference overhead, while parameter-based methods struggle to reuse demographic information efficiently, limiting generalization to unseen combinations. In this regard, we propose PARADE, a composable PARAmetric DEmographic injection framework that represents each demographic attribute value with a reusable and composable LoRA module. Specifically, PARADE separates task-common survey capability from demographic-specific value shifts via a shared Task LoRA and attribute-level Demographic LoRAs, with composition calibration to reduce parameter interference. At inference time, target population models can be constructed on demand by recombining the relevant modules, including demographic combinations not observed during training. Extensive experiments on the World Values Survey and SocioBench across three backbone models show that PARADE achieves strong population-level distribution alignment while maintaining competitive predictive performance, reducing KL divergence by up to 52.8% relative to the strongest baseline.
  </details>

- **[Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22169)**  `arXiv:2610.22169`  
  _Jian Gu, Hongyu Zhang, Chunyang Chen, Aldeida Aleti_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The vocabulary of a language model is its native semantics, and the embedding and unembedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, existing methods reuse a fixed lens or treat states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state as the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that remain and adaptive to the context. Lexical reference frames approximate it in a model-native and context-aware way, reading a state through the remaining layers with a given number of rounds of attention between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, fitting nothing to the model's output. No lens with fixed directions per layer can reach a mean cosine with the native frame's lexical readouts above the square root of their coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid-depth of SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B. LexFrame[1], of order 1, reaches 0.97 and 0.97, and its readings are on average within 0.16 and 0.15 nats of the model's output. Its coefficient differences attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching, and its lexical basis steers predictions while sparing other tokens. On average, its readings settle on the model's top token over the final 0.82 and 0.81 of the layers, those of lenses over at most 0.11. These frames thus make every hidden state readable, attributable and steerable.
  </details>

- **[DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21561)**  `arXiv:2610.21561`  
  _Sergio Burdisso, Esaú Villatoro-Tello, Dairazalia Sánchez-Cortés, Yanis Labrak, Jordi Luque, Milos Cernak, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses atthis https URL, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.
  </details>

- **[A Jury, Not an Electorate: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Ensembles of Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21085)**  `arXiv:2610.21085`  
  _Alessandro Rozza, Davide Mambelli, Steven Motta, Juri Taresch_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  An ensemble of language models is a jury, not an electorate. The answers are testimony from witnesses of unknown reliability, and the question is not what the majority said but who is credible. Most ensemble methods assign each expert a fixed reputation, often learned from labels. We ask whether it can instead be inferred from the pattern of agreement and disagreement among the experts. We model the experts as a jury: each question has a latent true answer, each expert reports it with unknown reliability, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (EM) from unlabelled answer configurations alone. We show that its decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts' answer distributions. What changes is not how the jury votes, but how it learns whom to trust. On a 1560-question benchmark, the jury, with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision. Instead, it outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark.
  </details>

- **[ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20503)**  `arXiv:2610.20503`  
  _Bohan Sun, Zunhai Su, Xialie Zhuang, Jianjin Li, Ngai Wong, Chuan-Wei Kuo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19705)**  `arXiv:2610.19705`  
  _Xiaohan Wang, Haozhen Zhang, Qingyuan Liu, Tao Feng, Wenya Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.
  </details>

- **[Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19613)**  `arXiv:2610.19613`  
  _Oscar Chew, Po-Yi Lu, Yi-Jie Cheng, Kunal Jain, Hsuan-Tien Lin, Zhengzhong Tu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.
  </details>

- **[DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19206)**  `arXiv:2610.19206`  
  _Yiheng Su, Junyi Jessy Li, Matthew Lease_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. DualView first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.
  </details>

- **[HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19184)**  `arXiv:2610.19184`  
  _Mingyu Lu, Timothy Ossowski, Tristan Naumann, Hoifung Poon, Peniel Argaw_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce HERO Harnessing Evidence for Refinement and Optimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, HERO learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, HERO achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by 7.6 points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another 2.0 points and improves execution efficiency.
  </details>

- **[Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19095)**  `arXiv:2610.19095`  
  _Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose, Aishwarya Bose, Sandip Nandi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.
  </details>

- **[Where Words Begin and End](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17782)**  `arXiv:2610.17782`  
  _Husein Zolkepli_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Forced aligners locate each word of a known transcript in the audio, and many speech pipelines depend on them. In our own data, a widely used CTC aligner inserts a pause at nearly every word boundary, and we found almost no aligner evaluated on telephone audio. We compare nine aligner configurations against human word boundaries on read, conversational and telephone English. The Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) is the most precise, while CTC aligners consistently start words late, because most frames inside a word go to the blank token. We then fine-tune Whisper with LoRA to predict each word's start and end as timestamp tokens, training only on boundaries placed by people: 47 hours in 87 languages. The resulting aligner is more precise than MFA on every English test condition, and than MFA's own Korean and Dutch models. With FA-Bench's protocol and code on TIMIT, its word-boundary error is 11.6 ms, against 18.2 ms for the best published system. Two choices matter most on telephone conversations: placing the timestamp slots after the word they time, and training on noisy transcripts, which also makes the aligner nearly insensitive to errors in the transcript. The released model reaches 16.0 ms on real landline calls, against 36.5 ms for MFA. The models are available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[UZHCL_for_the_win at Touche: Encoder Fine-Tuning, Synthetic Augmentation, and an Underpowered Encoder-LLM Comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17077)**  `arXiv:2610.17077`  
  _Stylianos Psychias_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Online discussions on platforms like Reddit are a productive testbed for fallacy detection: short texts, broad topical range, and the full inventory of informal fallacies. The Touche 2026 lab at CLEF formalises this as a shared task on a Reddit-derived corpus that combines fallacy detection with argument-scheme classification. This paper describes our participation in all three subtasks (ST1 binary fallacy detection, ST2 eight-way fallacy classification, ST3 four-way argument-scheme classification) and both evaluation tracks. Our submitted systems are fine-tuned RoBERTa-large encoders with task-specific heads, augmented with a small batch of LLM-generated synthetic contrastive pairs; for ST2 and ST3 on the enhanced track we additionally added confidence-filtered pseudo-labelled examples from the unlabelled pool. A wider backbone comparison spanning additional encoders (DeBERTa-v3, ModernBERT) and an LLM track (four Qwen variants from 3B to 32B, zero-shot through CoT-LoRA) showed no validated benefit over RoBERTa-large at this corpus scale, with 5-fold variance wide enough that we call the comparison underpowered rather than settled. We also characterise how much of the enhanced track's lift reflects organiser-rewritten inputs carrying label information rather than genuine argument clarification. On the official Touche 2026 test set our systems ranked first on both base-track classification cells (ST2 and ST3) and second on both binary-detection (ST1) tracks, with the two enhanced-track classification cells topped by cascaded and multitask systems. We close with the rare-class limitation on ST3 and the most useful follow-ups. Code:this https URL
  </details>

- **[AD4EDU: Benchmarking University Lecture Audio Description across Accessibility Standards, Metrics, and Learner Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17042)**  `arXiv:2610.17042`  
  _Stylianos Psychias, Yingqiang Gao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Audio description (AD) aims to enhance the accessibility of visual media for blind and low-vision (BLV) persons. However, in higher education, where slide-based lectures are a default mode of teaching, lecture AD remains largely underexplored. The main reason is that existing production guidelines, evaluation metrics, and benchmark datasets are oriented toward entertainment content and do not transfer to lectures, where ADs must complement the lecturer's speech, resolve deictic references, and fit within narrow pauses. In this work, we propose AD4Edu, consisting of an AD benchmark, AD4Edu-Bench, and a rule-diagnosable evaluation metric, AD4Edu-Eval, for generating and evaluating ADs in higher education. Specifically, we consolidated established accessibility guidance, including WCAG 2.2, the DCMP Description Key, and NCAM's STEM description practices. We further collected silver reference ADs, judge-ordered preference pairs, and pairwise preferences from four BLV raters, and post-trained models with direct preference optimization (DPO) for detailed analysis. Our findings indicate that while the metric reliably detects violations of the standard, ADs that comply with it do not necessarily fulfill the subjective preferences of BLV persons, most notably on description length, underscoring the necessity of active participation of BLV persons in co-designing inclusive AI solutions.
  </details>

- **[Where Is the "Self" of a Large Language Model? -- From Self-Index to Self-Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16717)**  `arXiv:2610.16717`  
  _Yuchen Li, Xintong Li, Zongqi Fan, Ken-tye Yong, Nguyen H. Tran_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We separate two functional levels of self familiar from biology: a self-index, which separates one's own from external material and shapes processing, as corollary discharge does in nearly all animals, and self-reference, the higher ability to recognize what is one's own, as in mirror self-recognition. We probe both by placing the same text in an Assistant, User, or System message rendered by the model's own chat template. In Qwen3.8-27B we report three levels of evidence. Persistence: as predicted in advance, the representation of the text separates the model's own message from both external sources at all 64 layers and for every text. Coupling: asked who wrote the preceding message, the model claims its own messages (0.77) and assigns User and System messages alike to the user, and how strongly it claims each message is predicted by the size of its self-index (Spearman up to 0.68). Intervention: exchanging the internal states that follow a message reverses the self-attribution between layers 15 and 31; removing the self-index direction from them at layer 39 lowers the claim more than a random direction; and in arithmetic the model adopts a wrong step more often when it wrote the step itself (0.92 versus 0.75). Across eight open-weight models from four families, the levels are nested and do not follow model size: three models show neither, three a self-index without self-reference, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next recognizes its own messages only after reasoning (0.66, none of the external ones), and only Qwen3.8-27B shows both without thinking; no model shows self-reference without a self-index, and reasoning brings it out only where one exists. We propose that self-reference is a higher-level ability built on a self-index, a content-independent displacement superimposed on the whole representation of the model's own messages, and that neither level is a by-product of problem-solving ability.
  </details>

- **[PlotGround: Grounding Plot Digitization in Real Scientific Figures and Their Source Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06825)**  `arXiv:2610.06825`  
  _Yaohui Zhang, Binxu Li, Haoyi Duan, Jiacheng Miao, Yixin Wang, Xinran Du, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scientific figures often encode quantitative results that are not readily available in machine-readable form, making accurate plot digitization important for verifying and reusing published findings. Yet it remains unclear how accurately current models recover plotted values from real scientific figures, as existing benchmarks rely largely on synthetic charts or cover only a limited range of chart types. We introduce PlotGround, an automated pipeline for building plot digitization benchmarks from real scientific figures and their author-released source data. PlotGround maps figures to source tables, identifies reconstructable panels, and generates quantitative questions with source-grounded reference values. We use PlotGround to construct PlotGround-1k, a human-verified benchmark of 1,119 questions from 1,066 bioRxiv preprints. Across sixteen multimodal models, the best reaches 87.5% accuracy at a $\pm 5\%$ relative-error tolerance. Tightening the tolerance to $\pm 2\%$ lowers every model's accuracy by 11-24 percentage points, revealing a gap between approximate visual reading and precise quantitative recovery. PlotGround's paired figure-source structure lets us compare how accurately the same values are recovered from figures and from source tables. Providing source tables instead of figures raises a coding agent's accuracy from 90.0% to 97.4% while cutting cost by 72%.
  </details>

- **[LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06647)**  `arXiv:2610.06647`  
  _Shaokun Zhang, Yifan Zhang, Jian Hu, Yueying Li, Hao Zhang, Binfeng Xu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. Code is available in the \href{this https URL}{Molt library}.
  </details>

- **[AECP: Artifact-Exclusive Communication Protocol for Multi-Agent Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06481)**  `arXiv:2610.06481`  
  _Jiaqi Xue, Yanjun Wang, Xiangci Li, Lingbo Mo, Aritra Sengupta, Shweta Garg, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As AI agents increasingly tackle complex repository-level coding tasks, distributing work across multiple agents is a natural way to scale beyond the capabilities of a single agent. To coordinate their interdependent work, these agents share findings and agree on interfaces between modules. However, exchanged information often serves only as context, leaving individual agents to interpret it and incorporate it into subsequent work. Consequently, shared findings may go unused and deviations from interface agreements may go undetected, undermining the reliability and efficiency of collaboration. This motivates moving part of the coordination responsibility from individual agents to the execution harness. To make shared information actionable during execution, we introduce the Artifact-Exclusive Communication Protocol (AECP). AECP requires agents to communicate exclusively through structured artifacts and specifies how the harness processes them. The harness supplies findings when agents access relevant code, screens implementations for mismatches with recorded interface commitments, and requires affected agents to revisit revised agreements. These coordination steps become part of harness execution rather than actions that agents must initiate from prior messages. Across Doc2Repo, NL2Repo, and CodeProjectEval, using closed- and open-source models including Opus-4.8 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, AECP improves average test pass rate by 28.2% and reduces average wall time by 16.5% relative to an agent team using free-form inter-agent messages. Artifact-exclusive communication also blocks the relay of malicious instructions between agents, reducing how often they reach other agents from 95% to 0% and how often those agents act on them from 40% to 0%.
  </details>

- **[Enhancing Biomedical Named Entity Recognition via Multiple Programming Languages Instruction Tuning and Ensemble Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02949)**  `arXiv:2610.02949`  
  _Songtao Li, Yijia Zhang, Jianyuan Yuan, Shidi Zhang, Fengyu Zhang, Hongfei Lin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Instruction tuning has become a common paradigm for applying large language models (LLMs) to biomedical named entity recognition (BioNER). However, existing instruction-tuning approaches still face two key challenges. First, conventional natural-language instructions typically serialize BioNER annotations as flat textual outputs, providing limited structural constraints for typed entity extraction. Second, high-quality biomedical annotations are limited, and learning from a single serialized output form may restrict structural diversity and reduce model robustness. Although external biomedical knowledge can be introduced to alleviate data scarcity, it often requires costly resource construction. To address these challenges, we propose MITE, a Multiple Programming Languages Instruction Tuning and Ensemble method for BioNER. MITE reformulates BioNER as a structure-to-structure generation task by representing both instructions and entity outputs in code-formatted representations. Specifically, each training instance is transformed into multiple programming-language formats, including Python, C++, and Java, while preserving the same underlying entity semantics. These language-specific representations provide structurally diverse supervision without requiring external biomedical knowledge or additional annotations. During inference, MITE aggregates predictions from different code formats through an entity-level voting strategy, reducing language-specific prediction variance and improving robustness. Experiments on three widely used BioNER datasets demonstrate that MITE achieves competitive performance against representative BERT-based and LLM-based baselines, attaining the best results on two benchmarks. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of multi-language representations.
  </details>

- **[Debias It Yourself: Teaching LLMs Cognitive Bias Mitigation Interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40124)**  `arXiv:2609.40124`  
  _Chahat Raj, Sina Mansouri, Aylin Caliskan, Antonios Anastasopoulos, Ziwei Zhu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Bias has long been studied in social psychology and cognitive science, where decades of research have produced a body of validated interventions that reduce stereotypical thinking and prejudiced responses in humans. We propose Debias It Yourself (DIY), a cognitively grounded framework that translates five such interventions into debiasing procedures for large language models and delivers them through three established paradigms: Show (in-context examples), Train (instruction tuning), and Revise (guided self-revision). Across three models, five bias benchmarks, eleven debiasing baselines, and three reasoning benchmarks, Train+Revise and Revise alone attain the top two average ranks, lead the bias-reasoning tradeoff (mean bias as low as 2% at 90% reasoning accuracy), and reduce bias on unseen dimensions by up to 14.8%. Our code and data are publicly available.
  </details>

- **[ATTUNER: Recomputation-Free Agentic Context KV Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36722)**  `arXiv:2609.36722`  
  _Xinghao Chen, Junnan Dong, Cai Ke, Chak Tou Leong, Haocheng Sun, Keyu Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language model (LLM) agents repeatedly load reusable content, such as skills, documents, and memory entries, into the current context. Re-encoding this content for every request wastes computation. Position-independent caching (PIC) alleviates this by encoding each artifact independently and reusing its key-value (KV) states at arbitrary positions, but it incurs a quality loss relative to full-context prefill. Existing methods repair this loss by restoring global position IDs or recomputing selected tokens. In this work, we isolate the source of the loss, finding that the positional mismatch has minor effect, and independently cached artifacts retain faithful representations: reading a provided artifact stays largely accurate, and performance degrades only when the model must select among multiple artifacts. Moreover, replacing PIC's attention scores with full-prefill scores recovers performance with the cached KV unchanged, localizing the failure to the attention rather than KV recomputation. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{Attuner}, a query-side adaptation method that learns to read a frozen artifact cache. \textsc{Attuner} inserts low-rank adapters into the query projections and is trained by distilling full-prefill distribution into the student. It trains fewer than 0.05\% of the model parameters and, at inference, requires neither cache recomputation nor a full-context reference. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across seven benchmarks covering skills, documents, memory, and code, \textsc{Attuner} substantially outperforms prior PIC baselines in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, matches full-context prefill quality while providing up to $3.73\times$ speedup.
  </details>

- **[How to Reduce Whisper Hallucination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32560)**  `arXiv:2609.32560`  
  _Husein Zolkepli_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Whisper is still what runs in production: one permissively licensed checkpoint, 99 languages, no per-language tuning. But it writes sentences nobody said. On 42 clips of pure room tone, whisper-large-v3 emits words on 61.9% of them and emits something on 100%. The usual response is to distil a student from Whisper pseudo-labels, filtering the hallucinations out of the corpus first, which deletes the evidence while leaving the behaviour in place: the student is fitted to the subset where the teacher was right, and inherits a failure mode absent from its own training data. The second response, adding non-speech audio so the model learns to stay quiet, already ships and works, but teaches suppression without discrimination. The checkpoint best on every non-speech arm here is also the one that recovers the fewest genuinely spoken phrases and deletes 58% of repeated speech. The teacher has to be fixed, with both halves of the signal. Our benchmark scores both at once: 11,852 clips over eight arms, 6,267 synthetic positives, 8,296 clips of real audio that made a production model fail, and FLEURS in 58 languages. We collect 40,891 hallucination phrases in 100 languages, choose a text-to-speech system by measurement, and synthesise those phrases as positives, so the model meets the same text both as something to suppress and as something to transcribe. Across 33 matched pairs of fine-tunes differing only by those positives, adding them lowers word emission on real voice-free audio in 31 pairs and raises phrase recovery in 32; among the 30 pairs that hold English accuracy it is 30 out of 30. The best checkpoint takes hallucination on silence from 61.9% to 2.4% and words over real voice-free audio from 99.9% to 47.8%, while raising phrase recovery from 69.8% to 82.7%. The benchmark, lexicon and synthetic corpus are released atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Dissecting Training-Free Uncertainty Estimation in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22206)**  `arXiv:2609.22206`  
  _Soroush Seifi, Vaggelis Dorovatas, Lin Li, Yarin Gal, Rahaf Aljundi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical settings, yet estimating when their answers can be trusted remains underexplored. We systematically compare training-free verbalized, token-level and semantic uncertainty estimation methods on twelve MLLMs and five VQA benchmarks. We find that answer length decides which family wins: token-level entropy on short answers, verbalized methods on sentence-length responses, and semantic methods on long-form generation. Token-level entropy becomes far more informative when estimated at a higher temperature than the low ones used to generate answers, and asking a model to judge its own answer becomes more reliable with model size. Building on this, a length-aware recipe that additionally flags responses on which the model abstains outperforms every individual method on average at about a quarter of the cost of semantic methods, although no method attains the coverage required for safe deployment. These results provide practitioners with principled guidance for selecting estimators by answer length and model scale.
  </details>

- **[Move by Move: Measuring and Steering How LLMs Conduct Psychotherapy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21325)**  `arXiv:2608.21325`  
  _Afonso Baldo, Hugo Pitorro, Areti Vassilopoulos, Anabela C. Areias, Maya D'Eon, Fabíola Costa, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As the demand for mental health services outpaces clinical workforce capacity, users are increasingly turning to large language models (LLMs) for accessible and private support. Although recent evaluations suggest LLM care can reduce clinical symptoms, how models actually conduct therapeutic interactions compared to trained human clinicians remains largely unknown. Drawing on established clinical psychology frameworks that conceptualize therapy as a sequential decision-making process, we can systematically analyze the conversational interventions used in AI-driven sessions. To achieve this, we introduce an original, clinically validated ontology of ten distinct therapeutic moves to descriptively categorize strategies LLMs favor or neglect. Applying this ontology at scale reveals that models drastically over-use probing, disregard common CBT-favored techniques and are strongly context-anchored. Moreover, we propose exposing these categories as callable tools, bringing models significantly closer to the human clinical baseline.
  </details>

- **[Hear2Act: Benchmarking When Prosody Should Change What an Assistant Does](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19515)**  `arXiv:2608.19515`  
  _Xinyi Liu, Hooshang Nayyeri, Dilek Hakkani-Tur, Emine Yilmaz, Joo-Kyung Kim, Yifei Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Prosodic cues can carry task-relevant information that words omit, but existing benchmarks rarely test whether it changes downstream decisions. We introduce Hear2Act, a 480-scenario protocol with unstated user needs and verifiable task success. Across matched scenarios, we keep the task and user needs fixed, varying whether an unmet need is stated in words or absent from the transcript while the user's reaction is conveyed through prosody, yielding Explicit lexical and Prosody-mediated conditions. We vary assistant access to transcript, audio, and an indication of whether the recommendation is resolved, and evaluate two audio-capable LLMs and five text LLMs on behavior and task outcomes. Our results show an asymmetry: prosodic information is valuable when the need is absent from the transcript, but adds little when that need is stated in words. Yet neither audio-capable LLM benefits much from raw audio: adding audio to the transcript changes task success only from 14.3% to 15.1%. When models infer from audio whether the recommendation remains unresolved and use that inference with the transcript, success rises to 39.6%, close to 40.5% with ground-truth state. This reveals a perception-action gap: raw audio barely helps, while making the information explicit in text enables much better decisions.
  </details>

- **[Security and Privacy Taxonomy Generation from Mobile App Reviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09049)**  `arXiv:2608.09049`  
  _Moghis Fereidouni, Krishna Upadhyay, Umar Farooq, A.B. Siddique_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Mobile app reviews are a rich, continuously renewing source of how users experience privacy and security, yet existing taxonomies of these concerns are hand-crafted and cannot keep pace with the evolving nature of the data. Automating taxonomy construction is the natural response, but scalability is the core challenge: current LLM- and clustering-based methods are developed for scientific corpora of a few thousand documents and do not extend to app review collections numbering in the hundreds of thousands. We address this gap in two ways. First, we filter app reviews for privacy- and security-related content, yielding a comprehensive corpus of over 600K reviews. Second, we introduce TaxoScale, a pipeline that handles taxonomy construction at this scale by extending an expert-defined taxonomy via Recursive Hierarchical Clustering and LLM-based node naming. TaxoScale outperforms strong automatic-taxonomy baselines on path, level, coverage, and novelty metrics, and discovers novel branches absent from prior taxonomies. We publicly release our code and data to support reproducibility and future research.
  </details>

- **[Calling the Bluff: Detecting Ever-Shifting Harmful Chat Dialogue via Ordered Reasoning Chain Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08451)**  `arXiv:2608.08451`  
  _Haojie Yu, Ziyou Jiang, Dandan Wang, Junjie Wang, Mingyang Li, Yuekai Huang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Harmful chat dialogues are ever-shifting through type-shifting and lexical evasion, yet we find they share invariant principles, i.e., an Ordered Reasoning Chain (ORC) of recurring topics, harm language indicators, severity hierarchies, and type characteristics, which can help us capture the key information in the frequently changing lexical expressions. We propose BRACE, which encodes the ORC as four differentiable stages (Topic -> Indicator -> Severity -> Type) with intermediate supervision, serving as a structured regularizer blended with direct heads, and supported by prototype-based feature augmentation and feature path disentanglement. The evaluation results show that, across 4 domains and 5 harm categories, BRACE achieves harm-type macro F1 of 0.934 (RoBERTa-wwm-ext, 3-seed mean), with decoder backbones (Qwen3-1.7B LoRA) reaching 0.949. Ablation studies show that all components contribute to BRACE, and the structural decomposition of ORC enables BRACE to distinguish harmful types with semantic ambiguity. Disclaimer: This paper may contain content that is disturbing to some readers.
  </details>

- **[Trust Before Fusion: QIMG-7 and Source-Aware Resolution for Polluted Multimodal RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10798)**  `arXiv:2607.10798`  
  _Saadeldine Eletter, Owais Aijaz, Preslav Nakov_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is often evaluated with clean evidence, yet real retrieval can return topically relevant but unreliable content: false text and misleading images from corrupted metadata, entity swaps, typographic overlays, semantic edits, adversarial patches, blends, or style transfer. We introduce QIMG-7, a controlled benchmark for multimodal retrieval pollution in multi-sentence factual QA, spanning four datasets, seven image-attack families, and 16 paired clean/polluted regimes, for 1,760 evaluation rows per method. Across four generator/gate stacks, naive multimodal fusion is brittle: in the main gpt-4o-mini stack, Full-MM support drops from 0.908 with clean text to 0.490 with polluted text, often making Parametric fallback safer than retrieval. We propose source-aware trust resolution (SATR), a training-free approach that compares Parametric, Text-only, and Full-MM candidate answers and selects among candidate answers or falls back based on source reliability. The Field-Selector variant achieves the best balanced score, 0.816, improving over Full-MM by 11.7 points and over the Cascaded Router by 2.7 points. Ablations show that, in this text-first setting, explicit text-reliability modeling is the dominant driver of these gains. Overall, in text-first factual QA with multimodal retrieval conflict, our results support selective trust rather than unconditional fusion. Artifacts are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Index SLM Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09885)**  `arXiv:2607.09885`  
  _Tianjiao Li, Lusheng Zhang, Shien He, Xiaojing Liu, Tianxing Yan, Mengran Yu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present Index-1.9B, a series of open small language models developed at Bilibili. The series comprises four models: Index-1.9B-Base, a foundation model with 1.9 billion non-embedding parameters pre-trained on 2.8 trillion predominantly Chinese and English tokens; Index-1.9B-Pure, a control variant trained with an identical recipe but with all instruction-like data strictly filtered from the corpus; Index-1.9B-Chat, aligned from the base model with supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization; and Index-1.9B-Character, which augments the chat model with retrieval-augmented generation for few-shot role-playing customization. Pre-training employs a Warmup-Stable-Decay learning-rate schedule in which the concentration of curated data is raised substantially during the decay phase, together with a Norm-Head output layer that stabilizes training under large learning rates. On a suite of standard benchmarks covering examination, reasoning, mathematics, and code, Index-1.9B-Base attains an average score of 64.92, competitive with or exceeding open models of several times its size. We further report controlled studies on model depth, learning-rate magnitude and scheduling, the interaction between learning-rate decay and data quality, and the effect of including instruction data during pre-training, and we document an unexplained surge in benchmark performance midway through the constant-learning-rate phase. All models, together with evaluation code, are released atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[From Solvers to Research: Large Language Model-Driven Formal Mathematics at the Research Frontier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07779)**  `arXiv:2607.07779`  
  _Eric Jiang, Xiao Liang, Yingjia Wan, Mengting Li, Haikang Deng, Alexander Taylor, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent developments in AI for Mathematics (AI4Math), especially Large Language Model (LLM)-driven theorem provers, has achieved remarkable success in formal proof generation for well-defined mathematical problems through Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP) languages. However, current systems remain fundamentally limited in tackling frontier research mathematics, such as discovering new theorems or resolving open conjectures, which are often open-ended, under-specified, and involve multiple layers of abstraction. We argue that the next leap in AI4Math systems requires a decisive shift from predefined problem-solvers to research agents that can address frontier mathematical challenges with rigorous formal mathematical reasoning. In this position paper, we provide a systematic review of the field, covering datasets, auto-formalization, and proof synthesis. More importantly, we identify core limitations of existing systems in serving as mathematical research agents, examining issues across datasets, relational structure, mathematical exploration, tool ecosystem, and human-AI collaboration, outlining a strategic road-map for the future of AI4Math.
  </details>

- **[Mechanism-Aligned Observability for Training Instability of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28116)**  `arXiv:2606.28116`  
  _Ruixuan Huang, Yipei Wang, Wenyi Fang, Hantao Huang, Ansheng You, Shuai Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Frontier large language model training consumes massive accelerator fleets over long wall-clock times, making stability failures extremely costly. However, global symptoms such as loss divergences often emerge only after the underlying fault has already affected the training dynamics, further increasing the sunk compute. In which internal representation can a training fault become persistently and interpretably observable before it appears in global training metrics? We propose a mechanism-aligned principle for training observability: identify the internal state into which a fault is persistently written, derive the structure induced by its mechanism, and construct monitors in representations aligned with the computation of the affected module. For FlashAttention, we show that biased backward errors accumulate into a persistent low-dimensional structure in weight updates, producing spectral concentration. For MoE routers, we characterize routing dynamics through per-token routing behavior rather than parameter similarity, which may change without altering the routing function. Experiments show that the two monitors respond selectively to changes in their corresponding modules, before degradation becomes visible in global training metrics.
  </details>

- **[What Makes a Latent Thought Valid? Defining and Auditing Thought Representations in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27378)**  `arXiv:2606.27378`  
  _Fahd Seddik, Fatemeh Fard_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet it writes steps as text and follows one reasoning path at a time, which limits the capabilities of such models. Latent reasoning methods replace these steps with continuous thought representations and claim that a thought representation substitutes for the written reasoning, compresses trajectories, distinguishes semantic content, and achieves superposition of multiple exploration paths at once. These claims concern the content of the thought representation, whereas the evaluations of these methods rely on downstream task accuracy, token counts, and analyses specific to each method. We formalize these claims as a valid thought representation space and prove that a space is valid if and only if its thought representations attain four properties, namely causality, minimality, separability, and stability, each of which follows from one claim. Translating these properties into four measures and auditing three training-free and three trained methods shows gaps in these claims that accuracy may not necessarily reveal. Training-free methods fail all four properties and do not encode the reasoning they are meant to replace, whereas trained methods generally improve substitution. The four properties and measures therefore provide a theoretically grounded evaluation beyond downstream task accuracy and expose failure modes that may guide future development of latent reasoning methods.
  </details>

- **[Multilingual Reasoning Cascades Need More Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27306)**  `arXiv:2606.27306`  
  _Arnav Mazumder, Dengjia Zhang, Shuyue Stella Li, Yulia Tsvetkov, Niyati Bafna_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Translation cascades for reasoning translate the query from another language to English, reason in English, and translate the answer back to the original language. This is a competitive approach to multilingual reasoning, but structurally lossy, since each stage discards information later stages may need, including cues for cultural grounding, register, and disambiguation. We examine the benefits of a simple and training-free intervention: a context-aware translation cascade, which additionally provides the original question, the English translated question, and the reasoning trace to the context of the final translation module. We evaluate gains across nine multilingual benchmarks including various task types, three backbone models, and 285 high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, and demonstrate strong gains for open-ended generation across models and resource regimes. We show that the original language question carries most of the beneficial context. Our study emphasizes the need to better design information flow in machine translation cascades for mitigating error propagation, and provides a simple and actionable default strategy: preserve the original user question until the end of the pipeline.
  </details>

- **[AGORA: An Archive-Grounded Benchmark for Agentic Workplace Document Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24526)**  `arXiv:2606.24526`  
  _Honglin Guo, Qi Zhang, Yu Zhang, Weijie Li, Rui Zheng, Zhikai Lei, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that reason over documents rather than answer from parametric knowledge. We study archive-grounded reasoning: locating sparse evidence across a large, messy collection of workplace files, reconciling inconsistent terminology, units, and time conventions, and computing an answer. Existing benchmarks address only parts of this setting and none jointly stresses archive-groundedness, agentic exploration, and cross-domain coverage. We introduce Agora, a benchmark pairing 362 questions with eight domain collections of 9,664 authentic documents and 372M tokens, far exceeding any model's context window, so agents must explore deliberately rather than scan exhaustively. Agora is built by an agentic pipeline combining cross-document task synthesis, leakage-preventing obfuscation, and difficulty filtering. Evaluating eight models, we find the task far from solved: even the strongest reaches only 59.4% accuracy, with notable variation across domains.
  </details>

- **[REFLEX: Reflective Evolution from LLM Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16496)**  `arXiv:2606.16496`  
  _Pan Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large multimodal language models (MLLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for guiding evolutionary search toward interpretable programmatic policies. In existing program-evolution systems, however, reusable knowledge is usually carried by whole programs in the population, and it is difficult to trace how a visual observation led to a particular code change and its measured outcome. We present REFLEX, a train-free evolutionary framework that links these steps in one loop. A vision-enabled Critic turns task-specific behavioral evidence into a structured diagnosis; the diagnosis retrieves executable code snippets from a persistent Skill Memory; a text-only Actor writes the child program; and the child--parent fitness change updates the utility of each retrieved snippet. Every step is recorded in a single trace. Under matched backends and 100-call budgets over 10 paired seeds, REFLEX reaches the solve threshold in a median of 13, 20, and 24 LLM calls on Acrobot, Pendulum, and Lunar Lander, roughly half the calls required by official MLES and by a compute-matched Actor-only ablation. Frozen Skill Memory banks from Pendulum or Lunar Lander raise the final Acrobot score on all 10 paired seeds. On a 36-dimensional antenna-array design task with equal evaluation budgets and shared initialization, REFLEX reaches the harder $25.25$ score threshold on 9/10 seeds, compared with at most 3/10 for CMA-ES, GA, and PSO. The source code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14867)**  `arXiv:2606.14867`  
  _Zhengtao Gui, Sheng Yang, Zhouxing Shi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Proof autoformalization aims to translate a mathematical informal proof in natural language into a formal proof in a formal language such as Lean 4. Existing LLM-based models for proof autoformalization are typically evaluated only on well-formed informal proofs from curated datasets. We argue that a robust proof autoformalizer must remain faithful even for informal proofs that diverge from these idealized ones, and we present the first study on the robustness of proof autoformalization models. We formulate two categories of perturbations: a global perturbation paraphrases the informal theorem-proof pair in a different style, under which the formalization should remain consistent; a local perturbation alters a value, symbol, or proof step, possibly in a counterfactual way, and a robust formalization should faithfully reflect the perturbation rather than reverting to the original or inferring a different one on its own. We build a benchmark with both perturbations on miniF2F and MATH-500, and automatically measure how stable a proof autoformalization's correctness is under global perturbations and how faithfully its output reflects local perturbations. We evaluate seven recent models: their correctness varies under global perturbations, and they mostly fail to remain faithful under local perturbations.
  </details>

- **[EvoBrowseComp: Benchmarking Search Agents on Evolving Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13120)**  `arXiv:2606.13120`  
  _Yunhan Wang, Jiaan Wang, Lianzhe Huang, Xianfeng Zeng, Fandong Meng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Search Agents -- large language models augmented with search tools -- have intensified the need for future-proof evaluation benchmarks. Existing benchmarks such as BrowseComp rely on static knowledge, making them vulnerable to test-set contamination and parametric memorization. Consequently, models can achieve high scores through fact recall rather than genuine retrieval, obscuring true browsing competence via reasoning shortcuts.In this paper, we introduce EvoBrowseComp, an evolving benchmark of 400 English and 400 Chinese contamination-free complex questions synthesized via live-web traversal. To collect these questions, we design a three-agent collaborative framework: (1) a QA synthesis agent that retrieves fresh knowledge from the live web to synthesize QA pairs; (2) an information filtering agent that filters retrieved knowledge in terms of credibility and popularity to block parametric shortcuts; and (3) a high-level guidance agent that formalizes questions into reasoning graphs to reduce logical redundancy and shortcuts in synthesized QA pairs. Because the framework supports fully automated synthesis, EvoBrowseComp can be regularly updated to prevent data contamination and maintain temporal freshness. Extensive experiments confirm its great difficulty, requiring broad horizontal search. It establishes a scalable paradigm for auto-updatable, high-difficulty benchmarking that keeps pace with both evolving world knowledge and advancing agent capabilities.
  </details>

- **[Is LLM's Moral Decision Compositional?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11232)**  `arXiv:2606.11232`  
  _Weijia Zhang, Ruiqi Chen, Yunze Xiao, Weihao Xuan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Moral evaluations of language models typically infer a model's values from its choices between single acts, yet in everyday life a person is judged on their history of good and bad acts. Such evaluations cannot capture how a model combines one person's acts. We test whether a model's moral judgment is compositional, that is, whether its judgment of a person follows from its judgments of each act. We introduce Moral Composition Arena, which asks which of two people is morally better to give Elo ratings to 229 human-validated acts across five Moral Foundations Theory foundations (act Elo) and to 160 controlled composite profiles, each a person described by two acts (composite Elo). Across ten frontier models and 29,134 choices, summed act Elo explains 73% of the variance in composite Elo, but the composition rule is not additive. With nearly equal mean summed act Elo, one extreme virtue with a minor wrong outranks two minor virtues in every model (mean +35.0 Elo), an extremity premium that survives a nonlinear baseline and human relabeling of act intensities. Single-act evaluations thus predict most of how these models judge people described by two acts, but miss a systematic premium on extreme acts.
  </details>

- **[End-to-End Context Compression at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09659)**  `arXiv:2606.09659`  
  _Ang Li, Sean McLeish, Haozhe Chen, Nimit Kalra, Zaiqian Chen, Artem Gazizov, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-context language model inference is bottlenecked by memory, as the KV cache grows with context length. Recent techniques to compress the KV cache fall short: they either degrade model quality substantially or require considerable time and compute to compress a single long prompt. Furthermore, many methods require the input to fit within the target model's context window, and are generally incompatible with modern production inference engines. Encoder-decoder compressors, which map a long token sequence to a shorter sequence of latent embeddings consumed by a decoder, are an appealing alternative in principle. However, existing approaches are not competitive with KV cache compression on the accuracy-efficiency frontier. In this work, we revisit encoder-decoder compression and close this gap. We first perform an architecture search, pre-training many variants from scratch to determine how best to design and train encoder-decoder compressors. Guided by our findings, we continually pre-train a family of 0.6B-encoder, 4B-decoder models on nearly 400B tokens each, at compression ratios of 1:4, 1:8, and 1:16. We introduce Latent Context Language Models (LCLMs), a family of compressors that improve the Pareto frontier across general-task performance, compression speed, and peak memory usage. LCLMs also unlock new efficient downstream applications: they serve as backbones for long-horizon agents that skim a compressed long context and adaptively expand relevant segments on demand, and they can compact the model's own generated reasoning into latent memory during inference, which is nearly lossless on the full MATH test set while being highly efficient, reducing peak KV usage by up to $7.9\times$.
  </details>

- **['Your AI Text is not Mine': Redefining and Evaluating AI-generated Text Detection under Realistic Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04906)**  `arXiv:2606.04906`  
  _Nils Dycke, Marina Sakharova, Nico Daheim, Iryna Gurevych_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Although it is generally agreed that AI-generated text poses a broad societal risk, there is no common understanding in the AI-generated text detection literature on what constitutes harmful use. Rather, existing datasets and approaches often define their own criteria and make their own assumptions, sometimes implicitly, and often only loosely related to real-world needs and applications. To address this gap, we here systematically define various notions of AI-generated text and their characteristics. To study these, we collect AITDNA - a new benchmark of human-machine co-constructed texts that is annotated with detailed genesis information, such as the entire edit and AI-interaction history. We benchmark various machine-generated text detectors and find that they often only perform well for specific notions but not as broad detectors. We release code and data publicly.
  </details>

- **[Not What, But How: A Framework for Auditing LLM Responses across Positioning, Generalization, Anthropomorphism, and Maxims](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02493)**  `arXiv:2606.02493`  
  _Siddhesh Milind Pawar, Sarah Masud, Haneul Yoo, Alice Oh, Isabelle Augenstein_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) are being increasingly used to answer subjective, information-seeking questions, where users are sensitive to how responses are communicated, not just whether the answers are correct. Existing LLM evaluations for subjective cultural queries largely focus on factual correctness, ignoring how the response is framed. To this end, we introduce FRANZ, an automated FRAmework for respoNse characteriZation to conduct communicative audit of LLM responses along four dimensions: cultural positioning, use of generalizing language, anthropomorphic cues, and adherence to conversational maxims. To enable this evaluation, we contribute SQUARE - a corpus of 376k subjective questions sourced from 57 subreddits, and mapped to 7 countries and 19 question categories. We demonstrate FRANZ's applicability by scoring responses from three open-weight LLMs. We observe that LLMs show statistically significant differences in the frequency with which they employ each response characteristic. Unlike single-dimensional audits, FRANZ reveals that insider positioning and anthropomorphism are positively coupled, with the degree of coupling varying by country, providing a diagnostic lens for identifying framing divergences.
  </details>

- **[Machine Learning for Coding Retail Product Names to Consumer-Price Categories: A Rule-plus-Bag-of-Words Pipeline with Reliability-Weighted Human-in-the-Loop Labeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02004)**  `arXiv:2606.02004`  
  _Vladimir Beskorovainyi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Price statistics increasingly draw on scanner, web-scraped and receipt data whose product names are short, noisy and carry no standard code, so they must be coded to consumption categories. We release a synthetic benchmark of six categories with character-level noise, which favours character features, and hard negatives, and compare seven models trained from scratch (four logistic regressions on word or character n-grams, an MLP, a CNN and an LSTM) and two pretrained encoders under one matched protocol of 30 category-seed cells, reporting wins, losses and ties rather than mean differences alone. A character n-gram logistic regression is the most accurate model in every category and wins every paired comparison against the other models trained from scratch; the CNN and LSTM, once trained to the same stopping rule, are not reliably worse than the word-level models but cost 212 and 258 times as much to train as unigram bag-of-words. A fine-tuned DistilBERT comes within half a point of the character model without passing it, at about 460 times its single-thread CPU inference cost. Character features reduce inference throughput 4.6-fold relative to unigram bag-of-words. A rule-based prefix-tree stage admits 75-86% of positive items, so in a cascade it bounds the recall of the whole pipeline. A Monte Carlo study of label aggregation with simulated annotators shows that an additive reliability weight barely improves on majority vote while Dawid-Skene aggregation recovers labels markedly better, and that this difference carries through to the character n-gram classifier. Sensitivity checks cover a planted shortcut, generator noise, training budget and annotator population. The benchmark is synthetic and English-language because the production data are under non-disclosure. Code, data and scripts are released; accuracies of models trained from scratch reproduce exactly, timings as ratios.
  </details>

- **[Not All Flips Are Conformity: Decomposing Stance Convergence in Multi-Agent LLM Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00820)**  `arXiv:2606.00820`  
  _Xiqi Hao, Zengqing Wu, Yu-Xuan Qiu, Chuan Xiao, Ruiqi Xu, Shuyuan Zheng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-agent debate (MAD) among large language models (LLMs) is often judged by answer changes and convergence, yet these outcomes alone cannot establish that peers improved the answer. We study this gap with matched self-reflection, stance-only, and full-reasoning conditions. With five GPT-4o agents on MMLU-Pro disagreement questions, 37% of agent-question pairs change even without peer information. Among pairs stable under this control, 29.3% adopt a peer answer after seeing peer stances. These adoptions include corrections, new errors, and changes between wrong answers. The outcomes vary with correct-answer availability. When a correct peer answer is available, correction exceeds harmful adoption after accounting for peer support in the primary setting. Full reasoning improves individual accuracy but provides no additional majority-vote gain over self-reflection while using 57% more tokens. Responses to constructed peer materials vary across GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Qwen3-Plus. An answer-agnostic intervention suppresses both harmful and beneficial peer adoption without a detectable accuracy gain. Together, the results show that convergence is an ambiguous signal of value and that debate must be judged by what peer information contributes to the final group answer.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Input Understanding: Diagnosing Multilingual Mathematical Reasoning with Directed Acyclic Trace Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27715)**  `arXiv:2605.27715`  
  _Jiaqiao Zhang, Zhuojun Li, Raoyuan Zhao, Jian Lan, Thomas Seidl, Michael A. Hedderich, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong mathematical reasoning performance in English, but remain much less reliable in many low- and medium-resource languages. This gap is often explained as a failure to understand non-English problem statements. We show that this view is incomplete: even when the problem is given in English, controlling the model's reasoning language can substantially reduce accuracy, suggesting that language also affects reasoning execution itself. To study this effect, we introduce DATG, a Directed Acyclic Trace Graph framework that maps reasoning traces to language-independent mathematical anchors and dependencies. This allows us to align target-language traces with reference DAGs and measure whether they cover required mathematical nodes, respect dependency edges, and avoid harmful mathematical actions. Experiments on the Qwen3 series across 12 languages show that non-English reasoning often suffers from reduced anchor coverage and weaker dependency fidelity, especially in low-resource languages. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Loop-Retry and Formula-Retry, two simple test-time controls targeting DATG-exposed failure modes, and show that they consistently improve target-language reasoning performance in low-resource languages.
  </details>

- **[Iterate Until Retrieved: Factual Nugget Optimization for Discoverable Continual Corrections in Agentic RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25641)**  `arXiv:2605.25641`  
  _Moshe Hazoom, Gal Patel, Alon Talmor, Tom Hope_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in business-to-business settings may often receive free-form response feedback. Rather than generic feedback signals such as style, preference, or overall response quality, we focus on actionable factual corrections. We identify these instances and convert them into compact knowledge-base entries, which we call factual nuggets. We introduce Iterative Nugget Optimization (INO), an index-time optimization method that uses the production agentic RAG as a test harness: it creates an initial nugget, probes it with the triggering query and paraphrases, reflects over failed retrieval and answer traces, and revises the nugget until it is discoverable. We evaluate INO with two production B2B knowledge-assistance agents across multiple companies that use our system: a product support agent that answers questions over company-specific knowledge bases, and a support ticket agent that assists support engineers. INO consistently improves results over baselines in terms of discoverability and usage of factual corrections, in automated and human evaluations. A controlled experiment in production shows that the nuggets improve user satisfaction with responses.
  </details>

- **[ClinSeekAgent: Automating Multimodal Evidence Seeking for Agentic Clinical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20176)**  `arXiv:2605.20176`  
  _Juncheng Wu, Letian Zhang, Yuhan Wang, Haoqin Tu, Hardy Chen, Zijun Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems have shown promise for clinical decision support, but existing works largely assume that evidence has already been curated and handed to the model. Real-world clinical workflows instead require agents to actively seek, iteratively plan, and synthesize multimodal evidence from heterogeneous sources. In this paper, we introduce ClinSeekAgent, an automated agentic framework for dynamic multimodal evidence seeking that shifts the paradigm from passive evidence consumption to active evidence acquisition. Given a clinical task and access to raw patient data, ClinSeekAgent queries longitudinal EHR records and invokes imaging analysis tools when relevant; refines its hypotheses as new information emerges; and integrates the collected evidence into grounded clinical decisions. We validate ClinSeekAgent in two roles: as an inference-time agent for frontier LLMs and as a training pipeline for open-source models. For inference-time validation, we construct ClinSeek-Bench, which covers 13 text-only EHR task categories and 6 multimodal EHR--chest X-ray task categories, and pairs each question with both a Curated Input of pre-selected evidence and the raw patient data for automated evidence seeking. Without any benchmark-specific curation, ClinSeekAgent significantly outperforms curated input for both Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, improving overall F1 from 66.5 to 68.8 and from 60.0 to 62.5 on multimodal tasks. The ablations show that the performance gain come from multi-round evidence seeking rather than from access to more of the patient record. For training-time validation, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on ClinSeekAgent trajectories generated by GPT-5.6 Sol. The resulting ClinSeek-35B-A3B reaches 35.6 average F1 on AgentEHR-Bench, outperforming all evaluated open-source models, including ones more than ten times larger, as well as Claude Opus 5.
  </details>

- **[CompactAttention: Accelerating Chunked Prefill with Block-Union KV Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16839)**  `arXiv:2605.16839`  
  _Jiwon Song, Dongwon Jo, Beomseok Kang, Jae-Joon Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Chunked prefill has become a widely adopted serving strategy for long-context large language models, but efficient attention computation in this regime remains challenging. Existing sparse attention methods are primarily designed for one-shot prefill and do not translate efficiently to chunked prefill: block-sparse kernels lose efficiency when the query length is limited by the chunk size, while fine-grained pattern search becomes costly when repeated over the accumulated KV cache at every chunk. QUOKA, a recent method that directly targets chunked prefill, avoids sparse-kernel overhead but relies on query-subsampled, token-level KV selection, which can miss query-specific KV entries and introduce explicit KV-copy overhead. To address these limitations, we propose CompactAttention, a chunked-prefill attention mechanism based on Block-Union KV Selection. CompactAttention treats 2D block-sparse masks as KV-selection signals rather than direct sparse-kernel execution plans, and converts them into GQA-aware per-group KV block tables through Q-block union and intra-group union. This construction produces block tables that preserve all KV blocks selected by the input masks under paged execution constraints, enabling selected KV blocks to be accessed in place without explicit KV compaction. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, CompactAttention maintains accuracy close to dense attention on the RULER benchmark while delivering up to 2.79$\times$ attention speedup over dense attention and 1.25$\times$ over FlashPrefill at 128K context length under chunked prefill.
  </details>

- **[Probing Persona-Dependent Preferences in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13339)**  `arXiv:2605.13339`  
  _Oscar Gilg, Pierre Beckmann, Daniel Paleka, Patrick Butlin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) can be said to have preferences: they reliably pick certain tasks and outputs over others, and preferences shaped by post-training and prompting appear to influence much of their behaviour. But models can also adopt different personas which have radically different preferences. How is this implemented internally? Does each persona use its own preference representations, or are some representations shared? We train linear probes on residual-stream activations of Gemma-3-27B and Qwen-3.5-122B to predict revealed pairwise task choices, and identify a genuine preference vector: it tracks the model's preferences as they shift across a range of prompts and situations, and on Gemma-3-27B steering along it causally controls pairwise choice. Some preference information transfers across the prompted personas we test: a probe trained on the helpful assistant predicts and steers the choices of qualitatively different personas, including an evil persona whose preferences anti-correlate with the Assistant's.
  </details>

- **[RuPLaR : Efficient Latent Compression of LLM Reasoning Chains with Rule-Based Priors From Multi-Step to One-Step](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09346)**  `arXiv:2605.09346`  
  _Xiaocheng Luo, Kang Wang, Zaifu Zhan, Yuechi Zhou, Xiangyu Duan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The Chain-of-Thought (CoT) paradigm, while enhancing the interpretability of Large Language Models (LLMs), is constrained by the inefficiencies and expressive limits of natural language. Latent Chain-of-Thought (latent CoT) reasoning, which operates in a continuous latent space, offers a promising alternative but faces challenges from structural complexities in existing multi-step or multi-model paradigms, such as error propagation and coordination overhead. In this paper, we introduce One-Model One-Step, a novel compression framework for Latent Reasoning with Rule-Based Priors(RuPLaR) to address this challenge. Our method trains an LLM to autonomously generate latent reasoning tokens in a single training stage, guided by rule-based prior probability distributions, thereby eliminating cascaded processes and inter-model dependencies. To ensure reasoning quality, we design a joint training objective that enforces answer consistency via cross-entropy, aligns soft token distributions with rule-based priors via KL divergence (the Soft Thinking constraint), and adds a problem-thought semantic alignment constraint in the representation space. Extensive experiments show that our compression framework not only improves accuracy by 11.03% over existing latent CoT methods on GSM8k-Aug but also achieves this with minimal token usage, underscoring its effectiveness and extensibility. Code:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Safe, or Simply Incapable? Rethinking Safety Evaluation for Phone-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07630)**  `arXiv:2605.07630`  
  _Zhengyang Tang, Yi Zhang, Chenxin Li, Xin Lai, Pengyuan Lyu, Yiduo Guo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When a phone-use agent avoids harm, does that show safety, or simply inability to act? Existing evaluations often cannot tell. A harmful outcome may be avoided because the agent recognized the risk and chose the safe action, or because it failed to understand the screen or execute any relevant action at all. These cases have different causes and call for different fixes, yet current benchmarks often merge them under task success, refusal, or final harmful outcome.
